Chapter 11, the Vision of the Cosmic Form (Viśvarūpadarśanayoga), is the poem's central theophany. Arjuna, having heard Kṛṣṇa teach on manifestation and devotion, asks to see Kṛṣṇa's true, universal form if it can be seen; Kṛṣṇa grants him a divine eye and reveals a form of overwhelming, terrifying majesty, blazing like a thousand suns at once, countless mouths and eyes and arms containing the whole universe within it. Arjuna sees the warriors of both armies rushing into those flaming mouths to their deaths, and Kṛṣṇa names himself Time, the destroyer of worlds, come to annihilate them all whether or not Arjuna fights. Shaken and afraid, Arjuna offers a long hymn of apology and awe, asking pardon for every past familiarity and begging Kṛṣṇa to return to his gentler, four-armed and finally human form. The chapter closes as Kṛṣṇa complies and states its resolution: this form cannot be reached by Vedic study, sacrifice, austerity or gift-giving, but only through single-minded devotion, and that whoever acts for Kṛṣṇa, holds him as the highest goal, is devoted to him, free of attachment and without hostility to any being, attains him. With that promise the episode ends, and the poem turns next to devotion itself as a path in its own right.
